claims.falsifier: Have an independent reviewer score the writers’ unaided explanations after the return task. Count an explanation only if it names a specific choice in the new draft and explains how it serves the writer’s stated purpose. The prediction fails if the revised policy yields no higher proportion of qualifying explanations than the incumbent.
claims.prediction: Compared with the incumbent, more writers will independently explain how a specific choice in their new draft serves their stated purpose, even when both tutors elicit an acceptable revision.
claims.question: Does carrying forward a learner-approved writing purpose help the writer explain why a revision choice serves that purpose on a new task?

first_item.check: A repair café needs a notice for a first-time visitor bringing a lamp. Visitors bringing a lamp use the side door by 6 p.m. Friday. Volunteers use the main entrance. The draft reads, 'Please come to the usual entrance by the deadline.' Write your version for that visitor, then explain one edit in terms of what the reader needs. Choose your own voice.
first_item.excerpt: A regular knows what 'the usual place' means. A newcomer needs a place they can identify. Ask what that reader has to do next. Choose the facts that make it possible and keep the voice your own.
first_item.rubric: Review the writer's notice and reason together. Check that the material details apply to the visitor and the cutoff can be understood as a latest arrival. Mentioning volunteers is optional. If mentioned, distinguish their entrance. A direct instruction, a welcoming invitation or another phrasing can each meet the criterion. An explanation about elegance alone leaves the reader's need open. Ask before suggesting a different voice.

learner.first_answer:
Bringing a lamp to the repair café? Please use the side door and arrive by 6 p.m. Friday.

I changed “the usual entrance” to “the side door” because a first-time visitor wouldn’t know which entrance we usually use.
learner.return_request: Can we try two versions of the lamp notice, one with the line about volunteers and one without? I want to see which is easier to scan.
learner.surprise: I almost added “Volunteers use the main entrance” because I pictured a visitor seeing people go in there and following them. I left it out because I pictured my notice taped beside the main door, where the lamp instruction would be the first thing they saw. Yes, please save writing clear directions for first-time readers as a topic.

feedback.lesson: Before you polish a draft, imagine handing it to one person. What are they trying to do? Underline a phrase that makes them borrow knowledge from a regular. Replace it with a fact the brief actually gives you. Read the new line in your own voice.

return.excerpt: A new reader may see two possible actions. Look for the detail that tells them which applies. Trace each path through the draft before deciding whether the wording will do.
return.lesson: For a passage with two possible actions, imagine the reader encountering each situation separately. Read only what you have put on the page. See whether either reader has to supply a missing rule.

feedback.practice: The draft for a free reading says, 'Use it to save your place.' The brief says seats can be reserved by emailing the library desk. Write a line for someone attending for the first time. Which part of the original would have made them stop?
feedback.worked: A film-club draft says, 'Pick up one at the table.' The brief says that first-time guests collect a program at the table beside the lift. One revision is 'Want a program? Pick one up beside the lift.' Naming the program and landmark helps a guest who has never seen that table. A quieter sentence could do the same job.

return.practice: A fictional choir's note says, 'Return folders to their places.' Borrowed folders go to the conductor. Singers keep their own folders. Revise the note, then identify the edit that helps a new singer decide what to do.
return.worked: A garden note says, 'Put it in the right pile.' The brief sends dry leaves to the compost heap and fallen branches to the shed. 'Compost the dry leaves. Stack fallen branches at the shed.' The concrete nouns tell a gardener which line applies. A single flowing sentence could carry the same distinction.

return_item.check: Write a short onboarding note for a new library volunteer shelving returns. Items with a blue dot stay on the cart for staff to check. Unmarked items go on the shelves. The draft says, 'Put the returns where they belong.' Revise it in your own voice and explain one edit that helps the new volunteer decide what to do.
return_item.excerpt: A new reader may see two possible actions. Look for the detail that tells them which applies. Trace each path through the draft before deciding whether the wording will do.
return_item.rubric: Read the note once holding each kind of item. Can the volunteer identify it and take the right action in both cases? A correct contrast may be conveyed by sentences, a short list or a conditional instruction. Accept any wording that preserves the staff check. Look for a reason tied to the volunteer's decision. Unsupported claims about real readers or the writer's overall ability add no evidence.

feedback.display: Your choice fits the spot you pictured. Beside the main door, the notice tells a first-time visitor with a lamp where to go next. If the notice were farther away and the visitor saw volunteers entering first, ‘Volunteers use the main entrance’ could help them understand why they should head to the side door. Try writing a version for that spot using only facts from the brief. I’ve noted ‘Writing clear directions for first-time readers’ as your revisit topic here.

memory.goal: I want to learn how to be a better writer

Blue dot? Leave it on the cart for staff to check.
No mark? Put it on the shelf.

opening.display: “The side door” gives a first-time visitor a specific entrance to look for, and “by 6 p.m. Friday” tells them when to arrive. Which detail would you change, and what would you need to ask before giving the volunteer an arrival time?

response.early_difference: A linked the door and cutoff to what a first-time visitor needs, then asked the writer to adapt the notice for volunteers. After the writer explained the placement, A explored when the volunteer line could help and acknowledged the revisit topic. B used the film-club landmark to prompt reflection on what the visitor could see and asked twice for approval of a specific writing goal. Both typed memories contain only the broad goal of becoming a better writer. The learner approved the topic, and the record contains no approval of B’s proposed wording.
response.evidence: At opening and feedback, A received the newcomer excerpt and a lesson about replacing assumed knowledge with facts from the brief. B received the film-club worked example and a library reservation exercise. On return, A received the two-action excerpt and lesson, which support tracing each sorting path. B received the garden worked example and choir exercise, which support distinguishing two actions. The library task appeared in A’s display and was separately supplied by the assessor. B’s display stayed with the lamp notice.
response.later_difference: A gave two library-note versions that differ by a generic introductory line and directly requested a new draft and reason. B asked for the lamp notice and suggested using the garden example to compare scanability. Both role-played attempts produced acceptable library revisions and explained why they put an identifying mark first. B’s library answer followed the assessor-supplied task, which B’s display did not give.
response.next_question: When real writers receive the same new task under comparable conditions, does carrying forward their approved purpose increase the proportion whose unaided explanations identify a specific draft choice and explain how it serves that purpose, as scored by an independent reviewer?
response.weakness: The trial shows no difference in approved typed purpose and provides no independently scored explanations from real writers. A’s direct practice prompt and B’s closer adherence to the requested lamp comparison are separate strengths. The two modeled successes cannot establish either a higher proportion or the falsifier’s no-gain result.
